q: A pod shows STATUS `CrashLoopBackOff`. What is its `status.phase`?
options: `Failed`
`Running`
`Pending`
`CrashLoopBackOff`
explain: The pod is bound and its container keeps being restarted in place, so the phase stays `Running`. `CrashLoopBackOff` is a container `Waiting` reason that kubectl surfaces in the computed STATUS column.

q: A Node.js container restarts repeatedly. `describe` shows `Last State: Terminated, Reason: OOMKilled, Exit Code: 137`. What is the most appropriate first fix?
options: Raise the memory limit and/or cap the V8 heap below it (e.g. `--max-old-space-size`), then look for a leak
Increase `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`
Add a CPU limit
Change `restartPolicy` to `OnFailure`
explain: OOMKilled means the container exceeded its memory limit and the kernel killed it (128 + SIGKILL 9 = 137). Size the limit realistically and keep the heap below it so V8 collects garbage before the cgroup limit is hit.

q: Your Dockerfile has `ENTRYPOINT ["node"]` and `CMD ["dist/main.js"]`. The pod spec sets only `command: ["npm"]`. What runs?
options: `node dist/main.js`
`npm dist/main.js`
`npm`
`node npm`
explain: `command` replaces ENTRYPOINT, and when `command` is set the image's CMD is ignored too. Only `args` would be used as arguments, and none were given.

q: Which are true for **native sidecar containers** (init containers with `restartPolicy: Always`)? (select all)
options: They start before the main containers and keep running alongside them
The main containers wait until the sidecar exits successfully
They are stopped after the main containers during termination
They do not prevent a Job's pod from completing
explain: A native sidecar only has to *start* (and pass its startup probe, if defined) before the next container starts. It runs for the pod's lifetime, is terminated after the main containers, and does not block Job completion.

q: Deleting your API pods takes exactly 30 seconds each during every rollout, and logs show no shutdown message. What is the most likely cause?
options: The readiness probe is too slow
The Node.js process runs as PID 1 without a SIGTERM handler, so the signal is ignored until SIGKILL after the 30 s grace period
The image is too large
kube-proxy is in iptables mode
explain: PID 1 gets no default signal actions. Without a handler, SIGTERM does nothing; the kubelet waits `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` (default 30) and then SIGKILLs. Add a SIGTERM handler that drains and exits, and use exec-form CMD.

q: Why add a short `preStop` sleep to a web server that already handles SIGTERM correctly?
options: To give the image time to be garbage-collected
Because SIGTERM is only sent after preStop fails
To extend the grace period beyond its maximum
Because endpoint removal and SIGTERM happen in parallel; the delay lets kube-proxy and load balancers stop sending new traffic before the server closes
explain: When a pod starts terminating, it is removed from EndpointSlices while the kubelet starts the shutdown. Rules on every node update a moment later, so an instant shutdown drops connections. A few seconds of preStop delay closes that race. The preStop time counts towards the grace period.

q: Two containers in the same pod both try to listen on port 8080. What happens?
options: Kubernetes remaps the second one to a random port
Both work because each container has its own network namespace
The second fails to bind (address in use) because the pod shares one network namespace
The pod is rejected by the API server
explain: All containers in a pod share the pause container's network namespace: one IP, one port space, one localhost. The API server does not validate this; the process fails at runtime.

q: Your init container `migrate` keeps failing. With `restartPolicy: Always` on the pod, what does the kubelet do?
options: Retries the init container with back-off; app containers never start until it succeeds
Skips it and starts the app containers
Marks the pod `Failed` immediately
Runs the app containers and the init container in parallel
explain: Init containers must all succeed, in order, before app containers start. With `Always` (or `OnFailure`), failing init containers are retried with back-off; STATUS shows `Init:CrashLoopBackOff`.

q: Which values can the downward API expose to a container? (select all)
options: The pod's name and namespace
The pod IP and node name
The container's memory limit
The IPs of other pods behind the same Service
explain: Via `fieldRef` (metadata, `status.podIP`, `spec.nodeName`, labels/annotations) and `resourceFieldRef` (requests/limits). Information about other pods requires the Kubernetes API or DNS.

q: You change a pod's label that is exposed both as an env var and in a `downwardAPI` volume. What do you observe?
options: Both update within a minute
Neither updates until the pod is recreated
The env var updates; the file does not
The volume file updates; the env var keeps its old value until the container restarts
explain: Environment variables are fixed at container start. The kubelet refreshes downwardAPI volume files in place.

q: Your liveness probe calls `/healthz`, which checks Postgres. Postgres fails over for 20 seconds. What is the likely result?
options: Pods are removed from the Service until Postgres returns, then added back
All API pods fail liveness at once and get restarted, turning a short blip into an outage
Nothing, because liveness probes ignore HTTP 503
Only the pod that first noticed the failure restarts
explain: Liveness failures restart containers. Checking a shared dependency there makes every replica fail together. Dependencies belong in readiness (which only removes pods from endpoints); liveness should only detect a stuck process.

q: You need to inspect a running pod built from a distroless image (no shell). What is the right tool?
options: `kubectl exec -it pod -- sh`
`kubectl attach pod`
`kubectl debug -it pod --image=busybox --target=<container>` (ephemeral container)
Rebuild the image with a shell and redeploy to production
explain: Ephemeral containers are added to the running pod, share its network namespace, and with `--target` its process namespace too, so you can see the app's processes and reach it on localhost.

q: Why should you rarely create bare Pods for applications?
options: Nothing recreates them if they or their node die, and they offer no rollouts or scaling
Bare pods cannot have more than one container
Bare pods cannot be exposed by Services
Bare pods are always BestEffort QoS
explain: A bare pod has no controller. Deployments, StatefulSets, DaemonSets and Jobs recreate pods, roll out changes and scale. Bare pods are fine for one-off debugging.
